en.title: Nonogram Strategy: Step-by-Step Guide to Solving Puzzles
en.desc: A detailed step-by-step tutorial on how to solve Nonogram (Picross) puzzles using logic and constraints, from basic overlaps to advanced techniques.
en.keywords: nonogram, picross, strategy, tutorial, logic puzzle, guide
en.author: Puzzle PK Team
en.content:
Nonogram is a fascinating logic puzzle game. This article will teach you how to use logic and techniques to solve puzzles step by step through illustrated examples.

Let's start with a simple 5×5 puzzle.

![Image](https://pica.zhimg.com/50/b0cf3a80d212e1e5c20a964dac2ac9f8_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

> **Tip**: Throughout this guide, **C** stands for Column (e.g., **C1** means Column 1 from the left), and **R** stands for Row (e.g., **R1** means Row 1 from the top).

We should always start from the easiest places. It's easy to see that Column 1 (C1) has only one valid way to fill.

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/2e56e67293ed775059d47adf19c65175_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Now Row 5 (R5) is also full. Looking at R1 and R2, since they require a block of length 3, and the starting point is given, it can only extend in one direction.

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/1e40f25a22e95e21254dad0c4785771a_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

The same logic applies to C2 and C3.

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/7e73b8ba337ebc6d23aed67520d164d9_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

We also need to fill R3.

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/50/090dabeefbbc9f32be126d548b0fc4ea_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

At this point, R4, C4, and C5 are still empty, and we can't get the answer immediately from their clues. However, since R1, R2, R3, R5, C1, C2, and C3 are filled, the cells we fill in R4, C4, C5 must not intersect with the empty spaces of those lines. This makes it easy to get the final result:

![Image](https://pica.zhimg.com/50/6fb3b04feb4e8ac6efcf7d4fd22c88ce_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

---

## Advanced Difficulty

Now let's increase the difficulty:

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/50/464ff5ca1cba61892a88b504a6dd54ef_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

First, R1 and R2 are the easiest to start with. The filling isn't unique, but obviously, some squares are mandatory in all possible configurations:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/503b97be157d90b0c02ab3f2cd5d87c8_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Next, C2 can be completely determined, and C5, C6, C9 can be partially determined. Also, R8C2, R4C5, R3C6, R4C9 definitely cannot be filled:

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/50/dd1fa5389e35d4b8ae9a53b1aa28657a_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Using the condition that R4C5 and R3C6 cannot be filled, we get:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/6dfcce5e8b7b76462cc8d4751eab247b_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

At this time, C3 already has a block of length 2, so the remaining filling is unique:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/a19d0552eebb44f7ddd2d9ea82becde3_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Since C3 cannot have any other squares filled, the first length 2 block of R1 and R2 is also determined:

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/50/5b689476c6493832a6ed83653d519b4a_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

C1 is determined, and the first part of R5 and R6 is also determined:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/fc7d66eabfc47ac45d914973399cb856_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

R7, C4 are determined (note that R5C4 and R6C4 cannot be filled):

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/cbb6ff4958643f2086fa9b374b030e60_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Determine R9, C5:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/3b955548757f1975f72c84476062d0a8_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

R10 is determined:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/7d6c7e2ab0f16e11364936843cd63192_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

For R1, R2, it's obvious that C8 can only contain a block of length 1. Thus we can deduce:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/9f84dac9931d10bbcc82041052e5f99e_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Now R1~R5, C1~C5 are all determined, and the rest is very easy to solve:

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/50/6809372b129b8fc5ec03264c6b821599_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

The final answer:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/2b661ddfeda917b4e9f342005f2fa2cd_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

---

## Core Nonogram Principles

The rules of Nonogram: The game board is a square grid where each cell must eventually be painted black or marked with an X. The goal is to find all the black cells.

Let's discuss the conditions under which an empty cell can be painted black.

### 1. Border Overlap Method
Every row or column has two extreme boundary ways of filling (packing blocks as tightly as possible to one end). When these two extreme fillings overlap, the overlapping region must be black.

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/dee3b38a51c35c8349537a9353220bae_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Consider C25. There are two ways to pack the blocks: either as high up as possible or as low down as possible:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/372d896d8208b12dcb91f51fe6c27240_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)
![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/f3b6f6adc782dcf3aaad8144518a1a3a_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

We can easily identify the overlapping regions for the two blocks of length 10:

![Image](https://pica.zhimg.com/4370a2fda042768ba333148a8f5f67c1_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

This gives us guaranteed filled squares.

### 2. Starting Point Extension
If the starting point of a certain length is given, the region extending from the starting point up to the length is black.

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/b37364b05ad5ca21c6a4d69ef9fd8b52_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

### 3. Closure and Exclusion
If a certain block length is fully determined, its two ends must be marked with an X.

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/3ef735467731f115eb51131031fa02f0_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Repeating these three basic methods gives us this state:

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/e5ef016f62d4c1199b69d252c1ff5426_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

---

## Core Strategy: Constraints

The overarching logic running through all methods is the concept of "constraints." A horizontal axis (or vertical) will inevitably be constrained by the other axis, limiting certain lengths to specific ranges.

Let's look at R1. C23 and C24 have provided their first blocks, both crossing R1. It is logical to deduce that R1C23 and R1C24 must be part of the final block of R1.

If we use the leftmost R1C23 as the starting point, it hits the border before reaching length 4, which is wrong. Therefore, to make this boundary case correct, the starting point must be at least R1C22:

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/70a843b8dc508c1adf2729edfd2ad923_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

The same logic applies to R2, R3, R24, R25:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/06143face1a3d10a3d96adae705f4882_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Due to constraints, newly filled black cells or X cells will impact the other axis, yielding this result:

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/b18e6a13a632bcbc3d5cb6dcfe81d6cc_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Now let's discuss the case where an area is **constrained by two X cells**. In C25, R21 to R25 is constrained by an X cell and the border. If this empty segment contains a block, it must be the length 3 block. We can then apply the overlap method to find guaranteed cells:

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/e497900068c0608e6ac82f89fa1ef512_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Similarly, R22C23 is constrained by two X cells, but since C23 has no length 1 block, it cannot contain any block:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/bce054ac05681665afbfd6e19a1ffa7b_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

After some patching up:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/9c19c02afa8745a61785bfd8b90fbdd0_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

---

## More Advanced Examples and Deductions

Let's use a new puzzle for further discussion.

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/f754542b9d0a271b5c0f71e5b599018b_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Repeating the previous techniques, we get:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/1a9c65db965c8255b43de998355644b7_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Let's look at C15, which contains blocks of 1, 9, and 3. For the final length 3, its possible range is constrained between R19 and R24. Therefore, R25C15 can never be reached and must be an X:

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/74507495c659681ede348ae6b3126111_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Applying this again:

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/721f4a5a221951d3ca6503a737d39d50_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

For R9, lengths 3 and 4 are determined, and length 7 is constrained to the two middle black cells. No matter how length 7 extends, there are unreachable areas, so:

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/531bcbe9b5e435b3377202a2676c7838_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

Now let's discuss **white cells surrounded by black cells**. There are two possibilities: they can either be connected or separated by an X.

![Image](https://pic1.zhimg.com/5cbf100bca8f539ebddc838a9a98b444_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

In C15, for R7C15 and R12C15/R13C15, if they were connected, the length would be less than 9. But we know R7C15 belongs to length 9, so they must be connected. Similarly, R13C15 cannot connect to R22C15, because R22C15 belongs to length 3.

By applying these advanced techniques systematically, we arrive at the final solution!

![Image](https://picx.zhimg.com/6ed5dc990cc82149e18a9f307d188785_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

zh.title: 数织 (Nonogram) 详细攻略：一步一步教你解题
zh.desc: 这是一篇从入门到进阶的数织（Nonogram/Picross）详细解题攻略，通过图文并茂的实例，一步步教你如何运用逻辑和技巧完成解谜。
zh.keywords: 数织, nonogram, picross, 攻略, 解题思路, 逻辑解谜
zh.author: Puzzle PK Team
zh.content:
数织 (Nonogram) 是一款充满魅力的逻辑解谜游戏。本文将通过图文并茂的实例，一步步教你如何运用逻辑和技巧完成解谜。

我们先来看一道比较简单的 5×5 的题。

![图](https://pica.zhimg.com/50/b0cf3a80d212e1e5c20a964dac2ac9f8_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

> **小贴士**：在后文的讲解中，**C** 代表列 (Column)，**C1** 即指从左往右数的第 1 列；**R** 代表行 (Row)，**R1** 则是指从上往下数的第 1 行。

我们要先从最容易填的地方下手，容易知道 C1 具有唯一的可满足要求的填法。

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/2e56e67293ed775059d47adf19c65175_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

这时 R5 也已经填满了。再看 R1、R2，由于这两行要求有长度为 3 的方格，且起点已给出，只能向一个方向延伸。

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/1e40f25a22e95e21254dad0c4785771a_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

再看 C2、C3，也是同样的思路。

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/7e73b8ba337ebc6d23aed67520d164d9_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

还要给出 R3 的结果。

![图](https://pic1.zhimg.com/50/090dabeefbbc9f32be126d548b0fc4ea_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

这个时候还剩下 R4、C4、C5 没有填，且这一行两列都不能立刻给出答案。但是由于 R1、R2、R3、R5、C1、C2、C3 已经填了，所以 R4、C4、C5 填的格子绝对不能被这几行穿过。这样就很容易得到最后的结果：

![图](https://pica.zhimg.com/50/6fb3b04feb4e8ac6efcf7d4fd22c88ce_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

---

## 难度进阶篇

现在我们把难度提高一些：

![图](https://pic1.zhimg.com/50/464ff5ca1cba61892a88b504a6dd54ef_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

第一步，容易知道 R1、R2 最好下手，R1、R2 的填法不是唯一的，但是显然几种填法都有几个方格是必填的：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/503b97be157d90b0c02ab3f2cd5d87c8_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

接下来 C2 可完全确定，C5、C6、C9 可确定一部分；且 R8C2、R4C5、R3C6、R4C9 必不能填：

![图](https://pic1.zhimg.com/50/dd1fa5389e35d4b8ae9a53b1aa28657a_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

然后利用 R4C5、R3C6 必不能填这个条件，可以得到：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/6dfcce5e8b7b76462cc8d4751eab247b_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

这个时候 C3 已经构成了长度为 2 的方格了，所以填法已经唯一：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/a19d0552eebb44f7ddd2d9ea82becde3_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

由于 C3 不能再填入其他方格，故 R1、R2 第一个长度为 2 的方格也确定：

![图](https://pic1.zhimg.com/50/5b689476c6493832a6ed83653d519b4a_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

C1 确定，同时 R5、R6 的第一部分也确定：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/fc7d66eabfc47ac45d914973399cb856_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

R7、C4 确定（注意 R5C4、R6C4 不可填）：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/cbb6ff4958643f2086fa9b374b030e60_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

再确定 R9、C5（如果都是利用不可填格使填法唯一，后面不再说明）：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/3b955548757f1975f72c84476062d0a8_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

R10 确定：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/7d6c7e2ab0f16e11364936843cd63192_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

对于 R1、R2，显然 C8 上只能填长度为 1 的方格。如果填 R1C10、R2C8，那么 C10 上要求的长度为 4 的方格则不能成立；如果填 R2C10、R1C8，那么长度为 4 的方格就会穿过 R5。所以可以确定：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/9f84dac9931d10bbcc82041052e5f99e_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

这个时候 R1~R5，C1~C5 都已经确定了，余下的就很好解了：

![图](https://pic1.zhimg.com/50/6809372b129b8fc5ec03264c6b821599_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

最后解出的答案：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/50/2b661ddfeda917b4e9f342005f2fa2cd_720w.jpg?source=1def8aca)

---

## 数织基本解题原理

数织的规则：游戏棋盘是一张方形格网，其中的每个格子最终需要涂成黑色或标记成 X。游戏目标是要找出所有的黑色方格。对于一道数织题目，它的每一个格子只可能有三种状态：黑格（必填）、X 格子（必不填）还有白格子（不确定）。我们的目的是把白格子涂黑或填上 X，使得白格子最终消失。

我们先来讨论在什么条件下白格子可被涂黑。

### 1. 边界重叠法
每一行或每一列都存在两种边界情况的填法（即尽可能地向一端靠近）。当两种填法的某一个长度有重叠区域，则重叠区域为黑格。

![图](https://pic1.zhimg.com/dee3b38a51c35c8349537a9353220bae_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

如图，我们考虑 C25 的情况。对于 C25 存在两种填法，即尽可能地往上“挤”或尽可能地往下“挤”：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/372d896d8208b12dcb91f51fe6c27240_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)
![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/f3b6f6adc782dcf3aaad8144518a1a3a_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

于是我们很容易知道两个长度 10 的重叠区域，故有：

![图](https://pica.zhimg.com/4370a2fda042768ba333148a8f5f67c1_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

这就是我们得到的最终结果。

### 2. 起点延伸法
若某一长度的起点给定，则从起点延伸直至长度的延伸区域为黑格。
由于我们需要根据起点和长度来确定黑格，故起点必依附于边界或 X 格。否则的话，从起点出发有两个延伸方向，那么就无法确定哪一个方向才是正确的了。类似地，如果我们知道了起点但是不知道它对应哪个长度，那么我们可以填上最小长度的黑格。

以上面的图为例子，显然我们知道 C25 上从 R4 到 R18 都是起点，且一定对应各自行的最后一个长度，故很容易得到：

![图](https://pic1.zhimg.com/b37364b05ad5ca21c6a4d69ef9fd8b52_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

### 3. 封闭与排除法
如果某一个长度已经完全确定，则它的两端为 X 格。
继续以上面的图为例子，由于我们通过起点确定了 R4 到 R18 的最后一段长度，故其两端即为 X 格（实际上右端为边界，但边界与 X 格是等效的）。于是我们得到如下的结果：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/3ef735467731f115eb51131031fa02f0_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

很快就得出一部分结果啦，为了方便我们把已经确定的长度高亮，然后重复上面介绍的三个基本方法：

![图](https://pic1.zhimg.com/e5ef016f62d4c1199b69d252c1ff5426_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

---

## 核心解题思路：约束

贯穿于整个解题思路的，是“约束”二字。和其它数字游戏类似，横轴（或者纵轴）必定会受到另一条轴的约束，使得该行（列）上的若干个长度被限制在一定的范围内。

首先我们看 R1 这一行。C23 和 C24 已经为我们给出了各自的第一个长度，且两个长度均穿过 R1，我们有理由相信，R1C23、R1C24 必定是最后一个长度的一部分。等价地说，R1 的最后一个长度必须包括这几个黑格，那么对于这几个黑格，存在两种边界情况，即以两个的端点为起点，向两个相反的方向延伸。

但是，如果以最左端的 R1C23 为起点，那么它还没延伸到长度 4 的时候就到了边界，这显然是错误的。因此，为了使这个边界情况的延伸是正确的，至少需要使起点在 R1C22：

![图](https://pic1.zhimg.com/70a843b8dc508c1adf2729edfd2ad923_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

对于 R2、R3、R24、R25 也同样如此：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/06143face1a3d10a3d96adae705f4882_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

由于约束，新填上的黑格或 X 格必定会对它所在的另一条轴产生影响，于是我们很容易得到如下的结果：

![图](https://pic1.zhimg.com/b18e6a13a632bcbc3d5cb6dcfe81d6cc_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

现在我们来讨论**被两个 X 格约束的情况**。如上图，R21C25 到 R25C25 被 X 格和边界约束住。如果这段白格包含长度，则这段白格必存在黑格。由于 C25 的长度 3 显然不可能在 X 格上方，故这段白格必包含长度 3。我们可以通过基本技巧第一条填出重叠区域：

![图](https://pic1.zhimg.com/e497900068c0608e6ac82f89fa1ef512_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

类似地，R22C23 被两个 X 格约束住，但是由于 C23 不存在长度 1，故不可能有长度被它包含：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/bce054ac05681665afbfd6e19a1ffa7b_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

修修补补：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/9c19c02afa8745a61785bfd8b90fbdd0_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

---

## 更多高阶实例与约束推理

我们继续讨论其他的情形，用另一道新题来讲解。

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/f754542b9d0a271b5c0f71e5b599018b_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

重复上面的技巧，我们可以得到如下结果：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/1a9c65db965c8255b43de998355644b7_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

现在我们还是以约束的思想，去看待一个简单的技巧。观察 C15，它包含了三个长度，分别为 1、9 和 3。而在 C15 中，有三个黑格已被确定。对于最后一个长度 3 而言，它的可能范围被约束在了 R19 到 R24，也就是说，R25C15 是绝对不可能被触及到的区域，即为 X 格：

![图](https://picx.zhimg.com/74507495c659681ede348ae6b3126111_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

再次利用基本技巧，得到：

![图](https://pic1.zhimg.com/721f4a5a221951d3ca6503a737d39d50_r.jpg?source=1def8aca)

对于 R9 而言，长度 3 和 4 已被确定，长度 7 被约束在中间的两个黑格。显然无论长度 7 怎么延伸，都有触及不到的区域，故有：

观察 C15，对于 R7C15 和 R12C15、R13C15，如果他们被连接起来，则长度小于 9，满足被连接起来的条件。但我们已经知道 R7C15 必属于长度 9，而包含 R7C15 的长度 9 即使是在边界情况也会连接上 R12C15；另一个条件是，C15 上的 R22C15 必属于长度 3，而显然 R13C15 和 R22C15 不可能连接，所以 R12C15、R13C15 属于长度 9。

en.desc: Master Five in a Row with essential tactical patterns — open fours, double-threes, broken sequences — and learn the positional concepts that separate beginners from strong players.

en.author: Puzzle PK Team
en.content:
# Gomoku Strategy Guide: From Random Play to Winning Consistently

Gomoku (Five in a Row) is one of the oldest and most strategically rich board games in existence. On a 15×15 grid, two players alternate placing black and white stones, with the simple goal of being the first to align five stones in a row — horizontally, vertically, or diagonally.

What makes Gomoku endlessly fascinating is the enormous complexity hiding behind this simple rule. A 15×15 board has 225 positions, and the number of possible game states is astronomical. The difference between a beginner and an expert is not raw intelligence — it is the mastery of specific tactical patterns and strategic thinking habits that this guide will teach you.

## The Three Levels of Gomoku Thinking

Before strategies, understand the three levels of tactical awareness:

**Level 1 — Reactive**: You respond to your opponent's last move. You look for immediate threats and immediate opportunities. Most beginners play at this level.

**Level 2 — Proactive**: You plan 2–3 moves ahead, creating threats that force your opponent to react to *you*, rather than the reverse. Intermediate players operate here.

**Level 3 — Positional**: You think about board control, influence, and the long-term configuration of stones across the entire board. Strong players always have a positional sense underlying their tactical moves.

The goal of this guide is to move you from Level 1 to Level 2, with an introduction to Level 3 concepts.

## The Essential Tactical Patterns

### Open Four (the Killing Move)

An **Open Four** is a sequence of four of your stones in a row with both ends open (unblocked). An open four **cannot be stopped** — no matter what your opponent does, you can complete five in a row on the next move. This is the most powerful forcing move in Gomoku.

Never allow your opponent to create an open four. The moment you see three consecutive stones with open ends, treat it as a direct threat that must be blocked immediately.

### Double Three (The Classic Trap)

A **Double Three** occurs when a single move simultaneously creates **two separate sequences of three stones, each with open ends**. Because each three threatens to become an open four, your opponent cannot block both threats in a single move — one will inevitably become four on your next turn.

Creating double-threes is the most common high-level attack strategy. Learn to identify positions on the board where a single stone placement would generate two simultaneous open threats.

### Straight Four vs. Open Four

A **Straight Four** (four in a row with one open end and one blocked end) is dangerous but can be blocked. Your opponent needs only one move to prevent it from becoming five. An **Open Four** (both ends open) cannot be blocked. Learn to distinguish these instantly — treating an open four as a straight four (and blocking only one end) is one of the most fatal mistakes in Gomoku.

### Broken Three (Sleeping Four)

A **Broken Three** is a pattern like `X_XX` or `XX_X` where the sequence is almost four but has a gap. It is a powerful setup piece because it is less obvious to the opponent than a clean three, yet just as threatening when combined with an adjacent piece. Learning to "see" broken threes — both your own and your opponent's — greatly expands your tactical vision.

## Defensive Principles

### Counter-Threats Are Stronger Than Pure Blocks

When your opponent is building a threat, consider whether you can create a counter-threat on your blocking move. A stone placed at position X that both blocks the opponent's three AND extends your own two to a three is worth twice as much as a pure block.

This principle — **defensive stones should be offensively useful** — is the hallmark of strong defensive play. Pure blocks that serve no offensive purpose should be avoided whenever an equivalent blocking position also builds something useful.

### Block at the Right End

When blocking a sequence, consider which end to block at. Blocking at the end that **also** extends or builds your own position is almost always superior to blocking at the other end.

### Never Ignore a Four

Whether it is a straight four or an open four, respond to a four immediately. Any other move you make instead will be irrelevant if the opponent completes five on the next turn.

## Opening Strategies

The opening in Gomoku (especially on a 15×15 board without swap rules) is critical because the first player has a structural advantage — they can always respond to any opponent move while simultaneously building a threat.

**Tengen (center) opening**: The center of the board (position 8,8 on a 15×15 grid) is the most flexible starting position. It maximises the number of directions available for future development.

**Corner proximity openings**: Stones played near the intersection of the board's quadrants (roughly 4–5 squares from centre) allow rapid development of diagonal threats, which are often harder for beginners to spot than orthogonal ones.

**Early diagonal development**: Diagonal fours are more dangerous than orthogonal fours because they occupy more "visual bandwidth" — beginners tend to scan for horizontal and vertical threats more naturally, making diagonal threats harder to see until too late.

## Board Control and Positional Concepts

At advanced levels, Gomoku is as much about **board control** as it is about immediate tactics.

**Central influence**: Stones played in the central region of the board project influence in more directions than stones played at the edges. A centre-dominating player tends to have more tactical options and can launch attacks in more directions.

**Thickness**: A cluster of your stones that faces open space (rather than the opponent's stones or the edge) is "thick" — it has potential energy for future threats. Thin positions (stones surrounded by opponent stones or edges) require defensive attention.

**Zone separation**: If you control one half of the board and your opponent controls the other, the game often comes down to which player can break into the other's territory. Understanding zone boundaries helps you decide whether to invade (risky, high reward) or consolidate your own zone (safer, but may cede initiative).

## Playing Against Different Opponent Styles

**Aggressive opponents**: Players who constantly push with chains of three and four need to be matched with counter-threats. Pure defence against an aggressive player usually loses — you need to create your own threats on the same move you block theirs.

**Patient/positional opponents**: Against players who build slowly and methodically, you need to probe for weaknesses rather than attack head-on. Look for moves that create double threats in positions they have undervalued.

**Unfocused opponents**: Many casual players will be building threats in one direction while completely ignoring a potential attack forming on the other side of the board. Scan the entire board for positions they may have overlooked.

## Practise with Purpose

**Solve Gomoku puzzles**: "Black to win in 2 moves" type puzzles are available online and in books. Solving these daily trains your pattern recognition for forced win sequences (miai, kyoko).

**Review your games**: After each game in PK mode, identify the turning point — the move where the game was decided. Was it a missed double-three? An overlooked broken four? This retrospective analysis accelerates improvement faster than pure play volume.

**Play both colours**: Strong Gomoku players are equally comfortable attacking (black) and defending (white). Deliberately practise from both sides.

Ready to challenge a real opponent? [Play Gomoku on Puzzle PK](/games/gomoku) — set up a private room and test your five-in-a-row skills in real-time PK mode!

zh.desc: 掌握五子棋核心战术形态——活四、双三、跳三——并学习区分新手与强手的全局布局概念。

zh.content:
# 五子棋策略指南：从随机落子到稳定制胜

五子棋是现存最古老、策略最丰富的棋盘游戏之一。在15×15的棋盘上，两人轮流落下黑白棋子，目标极其简单：率先在横、竖、斜任意方向连成五子。

让五子棋令人着迷的，是这简单规则背后所隐藏的巨大复杂性。15×15的棋盘有225个位置，可能的棋局状态是天文数字。新手与高手之间的差距并非智力，而是对特定战术模式和战略思维习惯的掌握程度——这正是本指南要教给你的。

## 五子棋思维的三个层次

在进入策略之前，先理解战术意识的三个层次：

**第一层——被动应对**：你对对手的上一步做出反应，寻找直接威胁和直接机会。大多数新手处于这个层次。

**第二层——主动进攻**：你提前规划2~3步，主动制造威胁，让对手被迫反应你，而非你去反应对手。中级玩家在这个层次运作。

**第三层——全局布局**：你考虑棋盘控制、影响力，以及全局棋子配置的长远走向。强手的战术操作背后始终有全局感作为支撑。

本指南的目标是帮你从第一层进入第二层，并初步接触第三层的概念。

## 必须掌握的核心战术形态

### 活四（制胜手）

**活四**是你的四颗棋子连续排列、两端均无阻挡的形态。活四**无法被封堵**——无论对手如何应对，你都能在下一手完成五子连珠。这是五子棋中最强的强制手。

绝不能让对手形成活四。一旦看到对手已有三子连续且两端均开放，必须立即视为直接威胁予以封堵。

### 双三（经典陷阱）

**双三**是指一手棋同时创造**两个独立的、两端均开放的三子序列**。由于每个三子都威胁成为活四，对手无法在一步内同时封堵两个威胁——其中一个必然在你的下一手变成四子。

制造双三是最常见的高水平进攻策略。学会识别棋盘上那些一步落子就能同时产生两个活跃威胁的位置。

### 冲四 vs 活四

**冲四**（四子连排，一端开放一端封堵）很危险但可以防守，对手只需一步即可封死。**活四**（两端均开放）则无法被封堵。要能瞬间区分这两种形态——把活四当冲四处理（只封一端）是五子棋中最致命的失误之一。

### 跳三（眠四的前身）

**跳三**是形如 `X_XX` 或 `XX_X` 的形态——序列几乎构成四子但中间有空位。它是强大的布局棋型，因为比整洁的三子序列更不容易被对手察觉，与相邻棋子配合时威胁同样巨大。学会"看到"跳三——不论是自己的还是对手的——能大幅扩展你的战术视野。

## 防守原则

### 反威胁优于纯封堵

当对手在构建威胁时，思考你的封堵手是否能同时创造反威胁。一颗棋子既封堵了对手的三子**又**将自己的二子延伸成三子，其价值是纯封堵的两倍。

这个原则——**防守棋子应当具有进攻价值**——是强手防守的核心特征。在有等效封堵位置同时能建立己方棋型的情况下，应尽量避免毫无进攻价值的纯封堵手。

### 封堵要选对端

封堵对手序列时，考虑从哪一端封堵。选择同时**扩展或建立己方棋型**的一端，几乎总是优于另一端。

### 绝不忽视对手的四子

无论是冲四还是活四，对四子序列必须立即响应。若你转做他处，对手下一手就可能完成五子，你其他的落子也就毫无意义了。

## 开局策略

五子棋的开局（尤其在15×15棋盘、不实施交换规则时）至关重要，因为先手方有结构性优势——可以在回应对手任何落子的同时建立自身威胁。

**天元（中心）开局**：棋盘中心（15×15棋盘的第8,8位置）是最灵活的开局位置。它最大化了未来发展所有方向的可能性。

**次中心开局**：落子于棋盘各象限交汇处附近（距中心约4~5格）的棋子，能快速发展斜向威胁——对新手来说，斜向威胁往往比纵横向更难被察觉。

**早期斜向发展**：斜向四子比纵横向四子更危险，因为它们占用了更多"视觉带宽"——新手倾向于优先扫描横竖方向的威胁，使斜向威胁更难在成势前被看破。

## 棋盘控制与全局概念

在高水平对局中，五子棋与其说是战术较量，不如说更是**棋盘控制**的比拼。

**中央影响力**：落在棋盘中央区域的棋子，能在更多方向上投射影响力，而非落在边缘的棋子。掌控中央的玩家往往拥有更多战术选择，能从更多方向发动攻击。

**厚度**：正对开放空间（而非对手棋子或棋盘边缘）的一组你的棋子，称为"厚实"——它蕴含着构建未来威胁的潜在能量。"薄"的棋形（被对手棋子或边缘包围）则需要防守关注。

**势力分区**：如果你控制了棋盘一半，对手控制另一半，局势往往取决于谁能打入对方势力圈。理解势力边界，有助于你判断是入侵（高风险、高回报）还是巩固己方区域（更安全，但可能放弃先手）。

## 针对不同风格对手的策略

**激进型对手**：不断以三子、四子序列施压的玩家，需要用反威胁来应对。对激进型玩家纯粹防守通常会输——你需要在封堵的同一步创造自己的威胁。

**耐心/布局型对手**：面对缓慢、有条不紊构建棋局的对手，需要探寻弱点，而非正面强攻。寻找能在他们低估的位置创造双重威胁的手段。

**注意力不集中的对手**：很多休闲玩家会专注于一个方向的棋型，完全忽视棋盘另一侧正在成形的进攻。每次行动前扫描整个棋盘，寻找他们可能遗漏的位置。

## 有目的地练习

**做五子棋死活题**：网络上和书籍中有大量"黑先两步胜"类型的题目。每天做题，能系统训练对强制胜利序列的图案识别能力。

**复盘对局**：每场PK模式对局结束后，找出转折点——那步决定胜负的棋。是错过了双三？是忽略了跳四？这种事后分析比单纯堆砌对局数提升更快。

**用黑白双方都练**：强手在进攻（黑方）和防守（白方）时同样从容。刻意用两种颜色分别练习。

准备好挑战真实对手了吗？[在 Puzzle PK 玩五子棋](/games/gomoku)——开一个私人房间，在实时PK模式中检验你的五子连珠实力！

en.content:
# Water Sort Puzzle: The Complete Beginner-to-Expert Guide

Water Sort Puzzle is one of the most satisfying logic games to appear in the past decade. The premise is elegant: you have a collection of tubes containing layers of coloured water, and your goal is to sort them so each tube contains only one colour. You can pour one tube into another only if the top colours match and the target tube has enough space.

Simple to understand, surprisingly deep to master. This guide covers everything from the core rules to advanced strategies that will help you breeze through even the hardest levels.

## Understanding the Rules in Depth

Before strategies, let us make sure the mechanics are crystal clear:

1. **Pouring rule**: You can pour water from Tube A into Tube B only if the top colour in Tube A **matches** the top colour in Tube B, OR if Tube B is completely empty.
2. **Capacity rule**: The amount of water poured equals the depth of the matching colour on top of Tube A. If the top 3 layers of Tube A are red, all 3 red layers pour at once into Tube B (as long as B has 3 or more empty spaces).
3. **Winning condition**: Every tube must contain only one single colour (or be empty). Partially filled single-colour tubes count as solved for that tube.

The key mechanic is the **batch pour**: multiple layers of the same colour always pour together as a unit. This is both a powerful tool and a major constraint — you cannot partially pour a same-colour stack.

## The Core Principle: Think in Columns, Not Moves

Beginners focus on individual moves ("I can pour this red into that tube"). Experts focus on **column state**: "After this sequence of moves, what does each tube's colour stack look like?"

The eventual goal for each tube is a single-colour column. Work backwards from that goal: which colours need to come together, and what moves need to happen to allow them to merge?

This is fundamentally the same type of thinking used in sorting algorithms — you are transforming a disordered state into an ordered one through a sequence of constrained swaps.

## Strategy 1: Create Empty Tubes Early

Empty tubes are the most valuable resource in Water Sort. An empty tube can accept any colour, making it a universal "buffer" that allows otherwise impossible moves.

In the early game, prioritise sequences of moves that **free up a tube** completely. Even if those moves look locally suboptimal (you are not directly sorting any colour), liberating a tube gives you the flexibility to make 3–5 more moves that would otherwise be impossible.

Experienced players always have at least one buffer tube available. If you find yourself in a situation where no tube is empty and no legal move makes progress, you are likely in a deadlock — meaning you need to undo several moves to create a buffer earlier.

## Strategy 2: Top-Down Colour Tracing

For any colour you want to consolidate, trace all its instances from the top of each tube downward. Ask:

- "Where are all the red layers on the board right now?"
- "Which of them are currently on top and can be moved?"
- "What needs to happen to expose the buried red layers?"

Consolidating colours that have few instances is easier than consolidating colours that are spread across many tubes. Tackle the rarest colours first — they require the fewest supporting moves and opening them up often creates cascades that help other colours too.

## Strategy 3: Avoid Creating New Splits

A "split" is when the same colour appears in two (or more) separate locations in the same tube, with a different colour sandwiched between them. Splits are the enemy — they mean you need extra moves (and usually a buffer tube) to eventually reunite the split colour.

Before making any move, ask yourself: "Does this move create a new split somewhere?" If yes, look for an alternative that achieves similar progress without introducing a new split.

Sometimes splits are unavoidable (especially in the early game with constrained configurations), but each split you avoid is a burden removed from the endgame.

## Strategy 4: The "Unsticker" Move

Sometimes a single colour is "stuck" — it is buried under other colours and cannot be accessed. To "unstick" it, you need to pour the blocking colours somewhere else.

The challenge is that pouring blocking colours might split them elsewhere. To avoid this:
1. Identify where each blocking colour's match is on the board.
2. Pour blocking colours **onto their matching colour** wherever possible, rather than into an empty tube.
3. Only use empty tubes to unstick a colour when no matching target exists.

This minimises the number of new moves required to clean up the temporarily displaced blocking colours.

## Strategy 5: Work from the Bottom Up

In any sorted tube, the bottom colour is the first that needs to "arrive." That means the bottom-most layer in your target tube must be placed first and must not be disturbed afterward.

When planning a sequence, think about the eventual sorted tube's colour from **bottom to top**: which colour goes in first (hardest to place, placed earliest), and which goes in last (easiest to place, can wait).

Counterintuitively, this sometimes means you delay filling a nearly-complete tube in order to free space for completing another tube that unblocks a critical sequence.

## Recognising and Escaping Deadlocks

A deadlock occurs when every remaining legal move makes the situation worse. Here is how to detect one:
- No move reduces the number of colour splits on the board.
- Every possible move requires using a buffer tube, but no buffer tube exists.
- You have been making moves that "cycle" the same colours around without making net progress.

If you are deadlocked, the only recourse is the **undo button**. Use it aggressively — undo back to the last decision point where you had an alternative path. The further back you undo, the more likely you are to escape the problem's root cause rather than just its immediate symptom.

## Level Design Patterns to Watch For

Hard levels in Water Sort often include these deliberate obstacles:

**Colour locks**: A colour that appears only at the bottom of multiple tubes, meaning it cannot be moved until multiple layers above it are cleared away. Identify these early and plan your first moves around excavating them.

**Tube fulls**: All tubes are at capacity, leaving no buffer space. In these configurations, your first sequence of moves must carefully choose which tube to empty first.

**Singleton layers**: A single layer of a rare colour sandwiched between common colours. These are especially tricky because you need an exact match available whenever you unbury them.

## Practice Mindset

Water Sort rewards patient, systematic thinking over speed. Resist the urge to tap quickly and undo repeatedly. Instead, before each move, take a breath and ask: "Am I creating or eliminating splits? Am I moving toward a completed tube or just shuffling colour around?"

The most satisfying Water Sort sessions are the ones where you plan a 5–8 move sequence in your head, execute it smoothly, and watch a tube click into perfect single-colour order.

# 水管排序攻略：从新手到高手的完整指南

水管颜色排序是近十年来最令人沉浸的逻辑游戏之一。设定极其优雅：若干支试管里装着不同颜色的水，你的目标是把它们整理好，让每支试管只含一种颜色。倒水的规则是：只有当源试管顶层颜色与目标试管顶层颜色相同（或目标试管为空），才能倒入，且目标试管必须有足够空间。

规则简单，精通却出乎意料地困难。这篇指南从核心规则到高级策略，帮你从容破解哪怕最难的关卡。

## 深度理解游戏规则

在策略之前，先确保机制完全清晰：

1. **倒水规则**：只有A管顶层颜色与B管顶层颜色**相同**，或B管完全为空，才能将A管的水倒入B管。
2. **容量规则**：一次倒入的水量等于A管顶层相同颜色的厚度。如果A管顶部3层都是红色，就会一次性将3层红色全部倒入B管（前提是B管有3格以上空间）。
3. **胜利条件**：每支试管只含一种颜色（或为空）。半满的单色管计为该颜色已完成。

**批量倒水**是核心机制：相同颜色的连续层总是作为一个整体被倒出。这既是强大工具，也是重要约束——你无法只倒出同色块的一部分。

## 核心原则：思考柱子的状态，而非单次移动

新手关注单次操作（"我可以把这个红色倒过去"）。高手关注**柱状态**："经过这一系列操作后，每支管子的颜色堆叠是什么样的？"

最终目标是每支管成为单色柱。从这个目标反向推导：哪些颜色需要汇合，需要什么样的操作序列才能让它们合并？

这与排序算法的思维本质上完全一致——你在通过一系列受约束的交换，把无序状态转化为有序状态。

## 策略一：尽早腾出空管

空管是水管排序游戏中最宝贵的资源。空管能接受任何颜色，是通用的"缓冲区"，让原本不可能的操作得以实现。

游戏早期，**优先规划能完全清空一支管的操作序列**。即使这些步骤看起来局部效益不高（你没有在直接整理任何颜色），腾出一支管，往往能为接下来3~5步原本不可能的操作打开大门。

有经验的玩家始终保持至少一支空管可用。如果发现自己处于"没有空管，且没有任何操作能推进进展"的局面，你很可能陷入了死锁——需要撤销多步，提前腾出缓冲空间。

## 策略二：从顶向下追踪目标颜色

对于你想整合的任何颜色，从每支管的顶部向下追踪该颜色的所有位置：

- "棋盘上所有红色层目前在哪里？"
- "哪些红色层目前露在顶部可以被移动？"
- "需要什么步骤才能暴露被埋住的红色层？"

整合出现次数少的颜色比整合分布在多支管中的颜色容易。优先处理**最稀少的颜色**——它们需要的辅助步骤最少，而且打通它们往往会触发连锁效应，帮助其他颜色也更容易整合。

## 策略三：避免产生新的分裂

"分裂"是指同一种颜色在同一支管中分成了上下两段，中间夹着不同颜色。分裂是你的敌人——它意味着需要额外步骤（通常还要借助缓冲管）才能在终局重新合并这个颜色。

在做任何操作之前，问问自己："这个操作会在某处产生新的分裂吗？"如果会，寻找能达到类似进展但不引入新分裂的替代方案。

有时分裂不可避免（尤其在配置受限的游戏早期），但你避免的每一个分裂，都是从终局移除的一个负担。

## 策略四："解卡"操作

有时某种颜色处于"卡住"状态——它被埋在其他颜色下面，无法被直接操作。要"解卡"，需要把压在上面的颜色移走。

挑战在于移走压层颜色可能会在其他地方制造分裂。避免这种情况的方法：
1. 找出每种压层颜色在棋盘上的匹配颜色位置。
2. 尽量把压层颜色**倒到与它相匹配的颜色上**，而不是倒入空管。
3. 只有在没有匹配目标时，才用空管来解卡。

这样能最小化为了清理被临时移走的压层颜色所需的后续步骤。

## 策略五：从底向上规划

在任何已完成的管中，底层颜色是最先"到位"的。这意味着目标管的最底层颜色需要最早放入，且之后不能被打扰。

规划操作序列时，从目标管的最终状态**从底向上**思考：哪种颜色先进入（最难放置，需最早规划），哪种颜色最后进入（最容易放置，可以等待）。

反直觉的是，这有时意味着你需要推迟填充一支接近完成的管，以便腾出空间来完成另一支打通关键序列的管。

## 识别与逃脱死锁

死锁发生在所有剩余合法操作都会让局面更差的时候。如何判断：
- 所有操作都无法减少棋盘上的颜色分裂数量。
- 每个可能的操作都需要空管，但没有空管存在。
- 你一直在执行让相同颜色反复循环的操作，没有净进展。

遭遇死锁，唯一的出路是**撤销按钮**。大胆使用它——一直撤销到上一个有替代路径的决策点。撤销得越深，越有可能逃脱问题的根本原因，而不仅仅是其表面症状。

## 关卡设计中的陷阱模式

高难度关卡常见以下刻意设计的障碍：

**颜色锁**：某种颜色只出现在多支管的底层，必须先清空上面的多层才能移动。及早识别这类颜色，让你的首批操作围绕"挖掘"它们来规划。

**满管窘境**：所有管都满载，没有缓冲空间。这种配置中，首批操作必须仔细选择先清空哪支管。

**孤立单层**：夹在常见颜色之间的某稀有颜色的单层。这类情况特别棘手，因为你需要在挖出它的时候，恰好有一个匹配位置可以立即接收它。

## 练习时的正确心态

水管排序奖励耐心、系统性的思考，而非速度。抵制快速连点、频繁撤销的冲动。每次操作前，先停一下问问自己："这步是在消除还是产生分裂？是在推进一支管的完成，还是只是在无效地移动颜色？"

最令人满足的水管排序体验，是在脑海中规划好5~8步的操作序列，流畅执行，然后看着某支管美妙地归一成单色。

en.content:
# Tetris Battle Strategy: How to Dominate in PK Mode

Tetris is one of the most played video games in history — but most casual players only ever experience the single-player version. The multiplayer battle variant transforms the game entirely, adding a strategic layer that most solo players have never even thought about.

Whether you are playing Drop (Tetris-like) in solo survival mode or racing a friend in PK mode on Puzzle PK, these strategies will help you think faster, stack smarter, and send more garbage to your opponent.

## Understanding the Core: The Stack and the Danger Zone

In solo Tetris, your only enemy is your own stack. In battle mode, a second enemy appears: **garbage lines** sent by your opponent whenever they clear rows. Understanding the interplay between your own stack management and incoming garbage is the foundation of competitive Tetris.

The "danger zone" — the top three or four rows of your playfield — is the trigger for panic play. The moment pieces start landing near the top, the clock is ticking. Panicked placements lead to poor gaps, which accumulate garbage faster, which makes the danger worse. Breaking this cycle requires learning to play both **efficiently** and **calmly** before the stack ever reaches the danger zone.

## The Fundamental Skill: Flat Stack Maintenance

The most important habit to develop is maintaining a **flat, low stack**. A flat stack means:
- Minimal "holes" (covered empty cells where no piece can naturally fill without rotation)
- No tall towers on one side that force awkward S or Z piece placements
- A consistent surface height that lets you preview pieces without being shocked by the next one

Developing a flat stack requires discipline during the easy early phase of a game, when it is tempting to place pieces quickly without thinking about the long-term shape. Spend one second per piece deciding not just where this piece goes, but where it leaves the stack for the *next* piece.

## I-Piece Management: The Key Resource

The I-piece (the long straight bar) is the most valuable piece in Tetris. It is the only piece that clears four rows at once — a **Tetris** — which is the highest-value attack in standard battle mode.

The conventional "keep a column open on the right for Tetris clears" strategy works, but requires advanced maintenance. Key rules for I-piece management:

- **Never bury the I-piece slot early**: If you leave the rightmost column empty for Tetris clears, keep the columns to its left below a safe height. If those columns tower over the slot, you can no longer slide the I-piece in.
- **Do not hoard I-pieces too long**: If you are waiting for I-pieces while your stack climbs, switch to clearing singles and doubles to buy time.
- **Recognise when to abandon the Tetris setup**: If garbage lines arrive and ruin your clean column, adapt. Continuing to try for a Tetris in a messy stack is a losing strategy.

## T-Spins: The Advanced Weapon

If you want to compete at a high level, you need to learn **T-spins**. A T-spin is when you rotate the T-piece into a slot that it could not reach by sliding alone — threading it into a tight space using the rotation system. T-spins generate significantly more garbage than a comparable row clear without spin, making them the premier attack move in competitive play.

The basic T-spin double (TSD) involves creating a "T-slot": an L-shaped hole with an overhang above it. The T-piece kicks in from the top, fills the hole, and clears two rows simultaneously — generating the equivalent of a 4-line clear in garbage sent, from only 2 rows cleared.

Learning T-spin setups takes dedicated practice, but even recognising *when a natural T-slot appears in your stack* and exploiting it is a huge advantage over opponents who miss these opportunities.

## Garbage Management: When to Send, When to Defend

Not all garbage situations are equal. Here are the key decisions:

**When to counter-attack**: If your opponent is setting up a large attack (you can see their board loading up), consider whether you can send garbage first to disrupt their plan. Sending garbage during their setup can bury their prepared holes, forcing them to scramble.

**When to defend**: When your stack is high and incoming garbage could end the game, prioritise clearing lines to drop your stack height. Do not try for Tetrises while fighting for survival — singles and doubles are fine when survival is the goal.

**Neutralising garbage**: In some battle modes, clearing lines while garbage is "pending" can cancel it out. If you see a garbage counter rising, a quick 2-line clear might neutralise 2 incoming lines before they land.

## Reading Your Opponent's Board

In PK mode, you can see a miniaturised version of your opponent's playfield. Use it.

- **High stack**: Your opponent is under pressure. This is the time to attack aggressively — any garbage you send now is hardest for them to manage.
- **Low, flat stack**: They are playing well. Focus on your own efficiency and wait for an opportunity to send a large burst (Tetris or T-spin double) rather than small inefficient clears.
- **Multiple gaps visible**: They are in trouble. Send garbage consistently to compound their problems before they can dig out.

## Speed vs. Accuracy: The Competitive Balance

New competitive players often assume speed is everything. In fact, **accuracy is more important at every level below expert**. An inaccurate fast placement that creates a covered hole will haunt you for the next 10 pieces. A slightly slower accurate placement keeps your options open.

The goal is to improve accuracy until the correct placement becomes instinctive, then gradually increase speed while maintaining that accuracy. This is the reason Tetris masters appear to play effortlessly — they have overlearned the correct placements to the point where deliberate thought is no longer required.

## Building Your Instincts: Practice Drills

**Sprint drill**: Play a 40-line sprint (clear 40 lines as fast as possible) daily. This builds raw stack management speed and forces clean habits.

**Opener practice**: Learn 2–3 specific opening sequences (a set of initial piece placements that build a stable Tetris setup from the random first 5–7 pieces) and practise them until they are automatic.

**Garbage response drills**: Deliberately play against opponents who send heavy garbage early. Learning to dig out from deep garbage piles (3–5 garbage lines) under pressure is the best teacher of efficient single-clearing and hole management.

Ready to test your stack management skills? [Play Drop 2048 and Tetris-style games on Puzzle PK](/games/drop2048) — compete in real-time PK mode and put these strategies to work!

zh.keywords: 方块对战, 俄罗斯方块策略, PK模式, T-Spin, 叠块管理, 竞技方块
zh.author: Puzzle PK 团队
zh.content:
# 方块对战策略：如何在PK模式中占据主导

俄罗斯方块是历史上游玩次数最多的电子游戏之一——但大多数休闲玩家只体验过单人版本。多人对战模式彻底改变了这款游戏，增加了一个纯单人玩家从未深入思考过的战略层次。

无论你是在挑战Drop 2048的单人生存模式，还是在 Puzzle PK 与好友进行实时PK对战，这些策略都将帮助你思考更快、叠得更聪明、给对手发送更多"垃圾行"。

## 理解核心：叠块区与危险区

单人俄罗斯方块中，你唯一的敌人是自己的叠块区。对战模式增加了第二个敌人：每当对手消行，就会向你的场地底部**发送垃圾行**。理解自己的叠块管理与来袭垃圾行之间的动态关系，是竞技俄罗斯方块的基础。

"危险区"——场地最顶部的三四行——是触发恐慌操作的信号。一旦方块开始落在场地顶端，倒计时就开始了。恐慌性放置导致更多缝隙，缝隙积累更快地增加垃圾，垃圾又让局面更糟。打破这个恶性循环，需要在叠块区到达危险区之前，学会**又快又冷静**地操作。

## 基础技能：保持平整且低矮的叠块区

最重要的习惯是维持**平整、低矮的叠块区**。平整叠块区意味着：
- 尽量少的"空洞"（被覆盖的空格，无法自然填入任何方块）
- 不要一侧出现高耸的柱子，逼迫S形或Z形方块只能尴尬放置
- 稳定均衡的表面高度，让你能从容地预判下一块

培养平整叠块区的习惯，需要在游戏容易的早期阶段保持自律——那时候很容易不假思索地快速放置，而不考虑对叠块区长期形状的影响。每个方块多花一秒，不仅想清楚这块放哪里，还要考虑它为**下一块**留下了什么样的落点。

## I形块管理：关键资源

I形块（长条形）是俄罗斯方块中最宝贵的方块。它是唯一能一次消除四行的方块——即**Tetris消行**——这是标准对战模式中价值最高的攻击。

传统的"在右侧保留一列空位用于Tetris消行"策略有效，但需要精心维护。I形块管理的关键规则：

- **不要过早封死I形块槽**：如果你在最右列留空用于Tetris消行，确保左边的列保持在安全高度以下。如果其他列高过槽口，I形块就再也无法滑入。
- **不要过度囤积I形块**：如果你为了等I形块而让叠块区越来越高，请切换策略，先消单行和双行来争取时间。
- **认清放弃Tetris设置的时机**：如果垃圾行破坏了你精心维护的干净列，请随机应变。在混乱的叠块区里继续强求Tetris，是输掉对战的常见原因。

## T-Spin：高级攻击武器

想要在高水平竞技中立足，需要学会 **T-Spin**。T-Spin是指通过旋转踢墙机制，把T形方块旋转到仅靠平移无法到达的缝隙中——实质上是"钻"进一个紧绑的空间。T-Spin产生的垃圾数量远超同等消行的普通操作，是竞技对战中最强的进攻手段。

基础的T-Spin双消（TSD）需要构建一个"T槽"：一个上方有悬挑的L形空洞。T形方块从顶部踢入，填满空洞，同时消除两行——仅消两行却产生相当于消四行的垃圾量。

学习T-Spin设置需要专项练习，但仅仅是能够**识别叠块区中自然形成的T槽机会**并加以利用，就已经比大多数对手有了巨大优势。

## 垃圾行管理：何时进攻，何时防守

不同的垃圾行情形需要不同的应对：

**何时反击**：如果你能看出对手正在蓄力大型攻击（他们的场地明显在积累），考虑抢先发送垃圾行打断他们的计划。在对手设置过程中发送垃圾，可能会封住他们精心留好的空洞，逼迫他们慌乱应对。

**何时防守**：当你的叠块区很高，来袭垃圾可能终结游戏时，优先消行来降低叠块高度。在为生存而战时，不要追求Tetris——单行和双行消除都是有价值的。

**抵消垃圾行**：在某些对战模式中，当垃圾行"待发"时消行可以抵消来袭的垃圾。如果看到垃圾计数器在增加，一次快速双行消除可能在垃圾落地前抵消掉两行。

## 读懂对手的场地

PK模式中，你能看到对手场地的缩略图，充分利用它：

- **叠块区很高**：对手承受压力。这是激进进攻的最好时机——你发送的任何垃圾此时对他们造成的伤害最大。
- **叠块区低且平整**：他们状态不错。专注自己的效率，等待发出大型连击（Tetris或T-Spin双消）的机会，而不是持续小打小闹。
- **能看到多个空洞**：他们陷入困境了。持续发送垃圾来叠加他们的麻烦，趁他们来不及挖洞逃脱。

## 速度vs.准确度：竞技的平衡点

新玩家往往认为速度是一切。事实上，**在专家级以下的所有水平中，准确度比速度更重要**。一次不准确的快速放置造成的覆盖空洞，会影响接下来的10块方块。一次稍慢但准确的放置，才能保持你的操作空间。

目标是把准确的放置训练到本能，然后在保持准确度的前提下逐渐提升速度。这就是为什么俄罗斯方块高手看起来举重若轻——他们已经把正确的放置位置训练成了不需要刻意思考的肌肉记忆。

## 建立直觉：日常训练方法

**40行冲刺**：每天练习40行冲刺（尽可能快地消除40行）。这能提升叠块管理速度，并强制养成整洁的操作习惯。

**开局练习**：学习2~3套固定开局序列（利用最初随机出现的5~7个方块建立稳定Tetris设置的放置方案），练到自动化程度。

**垃圾行应对训练**：故意选择会发送大量垃圾的对手进行对战。学习在压力下从深垃圾堆（3~5行垃圾）中挖出来，是学习高效单行消除和空洞管理最好的教练。

准备好测试你的叠块技巧了吗？[在 Puzzle PK 玩 Drop 2048 和方块类游戏](/games/drop2048)——挑战实时PK模式，把这些策略付诸实战！

en.content:
# Sokoban: From Beginner to Master — The Complete Strategy Guide

Sokoban is one of the oldest and most respected puzzle games ever created. Invented in Japan in 1981, its premise is brutally simple: push boxes onto target squares. Yet this simplicity conceals a depth of challenge that has captivated puzzle enthusiasts for over four decades.

If you have ever felt completely stumped by a Sokoban level — or worse, pushed a box into a corner and watched your solution become permanently impossible — this guide is for you.

## Understanding Why Sokoban Is Uniquely Difficult

Most puzzles give you room to backtrack or recover. Made a wrong move in chess? Take it back. Filled in a wrong number in Sudoku? Erase it. Sokoban is different: **boxes can only be pushed, never pulled**. A box pushed against a wall stays there. A box pushed into a corner becomes permanently stuck — an unmovable object that can never reach its target.

This irreversibility is the defining feature of Sokoban's difficulty. It turns every push into a commitment, and forces you to think ahead in a way that few other puzzle types require.

The official term for a permanently stuck box is a **deadlock**. Avoiding deadlocks — and recognising them before you create them — is the single most important skill in Sokoban.

## The Core Principle: Think Backwards

The single most powerful mental shift in Sokoban is learning to **think from the goal backwards to the start**.

Instead of asking "where can I push this box from here?", ask "where does this box need to end up, and what position does the player need to be in to make that final push?" Then ask what position the box needs to be in one step before that. Reverse-engineering the solution from the goal position dramatically reduces the number of paths you need to consider.

For complex puzzles with multiple boxes, extend this backwards thinking: "To place the bottom-left box last, I need the top-right box already in place. To place the top-right box, I need…" This dependency chain analysis is the hallmark of expert-level Sokoban thinking.

## Deadlock Recognition: The Five Patterns to Memorise

Before you push a single box, scan the board for these permanent deadlock configurations:

### 1. Corner Deadlock
The simplest: if a box is not on a target square and it touches two walls that meet at a corner (or the edge of the level), it is permanently stuck. Never push a box into a corner.

### 2. Edge Deadlock
A box pressed against a wall with no target along that wall — and with no way to pull it away from the wall — is stuck. Trace along the wall: is there a target square the box can slide to? If no, do not push it onto that wall.

### 3. 2×2 Square Deadlock
If two boxes are pushed together into a 2×2 formation and at least one of them is not on a target, the entire group is permanently stuck. Neither box can be pushed without the other being in the way. Watch for near-2×2 configurations and avoid completing them.

### 4. Tunnel with Dead End
A narrow corridor (only one cell wide) that has no target at its end is a one-way trap. Any box pushed into it can never come back out.

### 5. Frozen Box Chain
Sometimes a box is not stuck by itself, but becomes locked because of adjacent boxes and walls combining to form an unmovable cluster. Before pushing a box next to another box, check whether the combined pair would create a deadlock.

## Tactical Techniques for Specific Situations

### Prioritise Isolated Boxes
When a level has a box that can only be delivered to one specific target (because of wall configurations), prioritise solving that box first. Committing early to the forced assignments reduces the search space for the remaining boxes dramatically.

### Use Targets as Temporary Storage
Placing a box on a target that is not its "intended" target is allowed — and sometimes essential. The target marker simply disappears from view (or changes colour), but you can still push the box off it later. Use targets as staging areas when you need to manoeuvre other boxes past.

### Player Path Planning
Remember that you (the player) cannot teleport. The player character must physically walk to the pushing position, and those movements can be blocked by boxes and walls. Before committing to a push sequence, always verify that the player can actually reach the required position without disturbing already-placed boxes.

### Macro-Level Zone Analysis
Before making any moves, divide the level into zones based on which targets each box "naturally" belongs to. Draw mental lines connecting boxes to their likely targets, and check whether these paths cross. Crossing delivery paths always require careful sequencing — deliver in an order that avoids blocking your own later moves.

## Advanced Concept: Influence Analysis

Expert players use a technique called **influence analysis**: before pushing any box, mentally simulate how that push changes the player's ability to reach all other boxes. Does pushing Box A block the only path to Box B? Does it cut off the player's access to a critical corridor?

If a single push can strand the player in a sub-region with no way to reach a critical box, it is effectively a deadlock even if no box is literally trapped. This kind of "soft deadlock" analysis separates intermediate players from masters.

## How to Practise Effectively

**Start from the beginning, not the middle**: Sokoban's difficulty curve is steep and deliberately designed. Level 1 teaches specific patterns that appear in later levels. Skipping early levels means missing the vocabulary you need to read harder puzzles.

**Use the undo button freely**: In practice mode, using undo to explore different pushes is a legitimate learning tool. Experiment until you find the correct path, then replay the level from scratch without undo to cement the solution in memory.

**Think before you move**: Expert players often stare at a new level for 30–60 seconds before making a single push. Develop the patience to analyse deadlock risks before committing.

**Learn from failed attempts**: When you reach a deadlock, undo back to the last safe state and identify exactly which push created the problem. That analysis is the most valuable feedback loop in Sokoban improvement.

zh.content:
# 推箱子：从入门到精通的完整策略指南

推箱子是有史以来最受尊重的益智游戏之一。1981年诞生于日本，规则极其简单：把箱子推到目标格子上。然而，这种简单背后隐藏着极深的挑战性，让全球益智游戏爱好者痴迷了四十余年。

如果你曾经在某个关卡前完全束手无策，或者把箱子推进死角后眼睁睁看着局面无解——这篇指南正是为你而写。

## 为什么推箱子如此独特且困难

大多数谜题都给你犯错和纠正的空间。下错一步国际象棋，可以悔棋；数独填错，可以擦掉。推箱子不同：**箱子只能推，不能拉**。推到墙边的箱子无法移开，推进角落的箱子将**永远卡死**，再也无法到达目标位置。

这种不可逆性，是推箱子难度的核心所在。每一次推动都是一次承诺，迫使你以其他谜题很少要求的方式——向前多看几步——进行思考。

永久卡死的箱子状态称为**死锁（Deadlock）**。避免死锁，以及在制造死锁之前就识别它，是推箱子中最重要的单一技能。

## 核心思维：从目标倒推

推箱子中最强大的思维转变，是学会**从终点向起点反向推导**。

不要问"这个箱子从这里能推到哪里？"而要问"这个箱子最终需要在哪里，以及玩家需要站在什么位置才能完成最后一推？"然后再往前推一步：倒数第二步需要箱子在哪里？玩家在哪里？

从目标位置反向工程解题方案，能大幅减少你需要考虑的路径数量。

对于有多个箱子的复杂关卡，同样可以延伸这种逆向思维："要最后放好左下角的箱子，我需要右上角的箱子已经就位。要让右上角的箱子就位，我需要……"这种依赖链分析，是高手级推箱子思维的标志。

## 死锁识别：必须记住的五种模式

在推任何箱子之前，先扫描棋盘上是否存在以下永久性死锁配置：

### 1. 角落死锁
最简单的情形：一个箱子不在目标格上，同时紧靠两面相交的墙壁（或关卡边缘形成的角落），则永久卡死。永远不要把箱子推进角落。

### 2. 边缘死锁
箱子紧靠一面墙，而那面墙上没有目标格、也没有办法把箱子从墙上拉开。沿着墙追踪：箱子能否沿墙滑动到某个目标？如果不能，就不要把它推到那面墙上。

### 3. 2×2 方块死锁
两个箱子被推到一起，形成2×2的方形，只要其中一个不在目标格上，整组箱子就永久卡死——因为任何一个都挡住了另一个的路。推箱子前要检查会不会完成这种"田"字形。

### 4. 死路隧道
只有一格宽的走廊，尽头没有目标格，就是一条单行的死路。任何被推进去的箱子都永远出不来。

### 5. 冻结链
有时一个箱子本身不卡死，但相邻的其他箱子和墙壁组合起来，形成一个无法移动的整体。把一个箱子推到另一箱子旁边之前，检查这两个组合起来是否会制造死锁。

## 特定情形的战术技巧

### 优先解决孤立箱子
当一个箱子因为墙壁配置，只能送到唯一的目标格时，先解决它。把"强制分配"的箱子优先搞定，可以大幅减少剩余箱子的搜索空间。

### 把已完成的目标格用作临时中转
把一个箱子放在"并非它最终目标"的目标格上，是允许的，也是有时必须的。目标格的标记只是不再显示，但你之后还能把那个箱子推走。在需要机动其他箱子经过某处时，把目标格当作暂时的中转站。

### 规划玩家的行走路径
记住，玩家本身不能瞬移。玩家角色必须实际走到推箱子的位置，而这些走动可能被箱子和墙壁阻挡。在确定一个推动序列之前，始终验证玩家能否在不干扰已放好的箱子的情况下，实际到达所需位置。

### 宏观区域分析
在做任何动作之前，把关卡按照各箱子"自然对应"的目标分成几个区域。在脑海中画出连接箱子和目标的线段，检查这些路径是否交叉。路径交叉意味着需要仔细的先后顺序——按照不阻挡后续操作的顺序来放置。

## 高级概念：影响力分析

高手会使用一种叫做**影响力分析**的技巧：在推任何箱子之前，在脑海中模拟这次推动如何改变玩家到达所有其他箱子的能力。推动A箱，是否会堵死通向B箱的唯一路径？是否会切断进入关键通道的入口？

如果一次推动可能让玩家困在一个无法接触到某个关键箱子的区域，这实际上就是死锁——即使没有箱子被字面意义上卡住。这种"软死锁"分析，是区别中级玩家和高手的关键。

## 如何高效练习

**从第一关开始，不要跳过**：推箱子的难度曲线陡峭且经过精心设计。第1关教的模式会反复出现在后面的关卡中。跳过早期关卡，意味着缺失读懂后续谜题所需的"词汇量"。

**大胆使用撤销**：在练习中，用撤销键探索不同推法是完全合理的学习工具。找到正确路径后，从头再玩一遍，不用撤销，把解法刻入记忆。

**推之前先思考**：高手在看到新关卡后，往往会静静分析30~60秒再动手。培养在承诺之前分析死锁风险的耐心。

**从失败中学习**：每次遭遇死锁，撤销回最后的安全状态，确切找出是哪一步推动制造了问题。这种分析是推箱子进步最有价值的反馈循环。

准备好把这些策略付诸实战了吗？[在 Puzzle PK 玩推箱子](/games/sokoban)，200多个精心设计的关卡，从入门到专家难度一应俱全。单人闯关，或与好友实时PK竞速！

en.content:
# The Hidden Logic of Minesweeper: A Complete Strategy Guide

Most casual players treat Minesweeper as a game of luck, clicking randomly until they inevitably hit a mine. But beneath its simple exterior lies a game of **pure logic and probability**. Master these techniques and you will win consistently — no guessing required.

## Understanding the Foundation

The core of Minesweeper is deceptively simple: the number on a revealed square tells you exactly how many mines are adjacent to it (horizontally, vertically, and diagonally). A "1" means exactly one mine among its neighbours. A "2" means two mines. Understanding this single rule is the foundation of everything else.

Before diving into patterns, learn the two fundamental actions:
- **Flag a square**: When you are certain a square contains a mine, right-click to flag it.
- **Chord**: When a numbered square has exactly as many flags adjacent to it as its number, you can middle-click (or double-click on mobile) to automatically reveal all unflagged neighbours. This is the single fastest technique in the game.

## The Essential Patterns

### The 1-1 Pattern (Wall Rule)

This is the most common pattern you will encounter. When you see two "1"s sitting side by side against an unrevealed wall, the square that only the second "1" can see is always **safe**.

**Example**: `[1][1]` with three unrevealed squares along the wall — the outer two squares belong exclusively to each "1", so the mine must be one of the two inner shared squares. The outermost square is safe to click.

This pattern can be extended: `[1][1][1][1]` along a wall means the mine alternates in a predictable way, allowing you to chain-clear large sections.

### The 1-2 Pattern

When a "1" is adjacent to a "2", and both border the same wall of unrevealed squares, you gain powerful information:

- The "1" tells you: exactly one mine among my two unrevealed neighbours.
- The "2" tells you: exactly two mines among my three unrevealed neighbours.
- Subtracting: the square the "2" sees that the "1" does **not** see must contain **exactly one mine**.

Mastering the subtraction technique — where you mentally subtract one constraint from another — unlocks the vast majority of Minesweeper deductions.

### The 1-2-1 Pattern

When you see `[1][2][1]` against a flat wall, the mines are **always** directly opposite the two "1"s. The square opposite the "2" is always safe. This is incredibly reliable and appears in nearly every game.

### The 1-2-2-1 Pattern

Similar to 1-2-1, this pattern dictates that mines are located opposite the two "2"s, while the squares opposite the "1"s are safe. Once you recognise this shape instantly, you will find yourself solving boards in seconds.

## Corner and Edge Strategies

**Corners** are powerful starting points. A "1" in a corner can only have one adjacent unrevealed square in many situations, immediately telling you where (or where not) the mine is.

**Edges** reduce each square's neighbour count, making each number more informative. When a "3" appears on the edge, it has fewer neighbours — its constraint is tighter and easier to resolve.

When you open a game, if the first click reveals a zero (a blank square), a large area will cascade-clear automatically. Try clicking near the centre of the board; statistically, this gives you the best chance of opening a large blank region and revealing many numbers at once.

## Advanced Techniques: Probability and Counting

When pure logic is exhausted and you must guess, you can still be smart about it.

### Mine Counting

At any point in the game, you know the total number of mines on the board (shown in the counter). As you flag mines, the counter decrements. By subtracting flagged mines from the total, you know how many remain. If only a few unrevealed squares remain and you know the mine count, you can sometimes determine exact locations purely by arithmetic.

### Probability Estimation

When forced to guess, estimate probabilities rather than clicking blindly:
- An isolated square in the corner might have a 1-in-2 (50%) mine chance.
- A square in the open field surrounded by many zeros might only have a 10–15% mine chance based on the overall mine density.
- Always choose the **lowest-probability** square when guessing.

### The Boundary Technique

Expert players divide the board into "constrained" squares (those adjacent to numbers) and "unconstrained" squares (those completely isolated from numbered cells). Unconstrained squares all share the same uniform mine probability: `remaining_mines / remaining_unrevealed_unconstrained_squares`. Compare this to the calculated probabilities in constrained regions — sometimes the open field is safer than it looks.

## Speed Techniques for PK Mode

In Puzzle PK's multiplayer PK mode, speed matters as much as accuracy. Here are speed-focused tips:

- **Use chording aggressively**: The moment you flag a mine adjacent to a satisfied number, immediately chord that number. Chain chords propagate through the board like dominoes.
- **Keep your mouse moving**: Don't stop and think for long. Do quick mental scans, flag the obvious mines, and keep momentum.
- **Left-right click simultaneously (classic chord)**: On desktop, holding both mouse buttons down on a number that has its mine count satisfied will auto-reveal — even faster than middle-clicking.
- **Memorise board layouts**: In PK Steal mode, both players share the same board. Watch where your opponent clicks — their revealed squares give you extra information too.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

1. **Flagging too eagerly**: Some players reflexively flag every suspected mine. This slows you down. Only flag when you need that flag to trigger a chord later.
2. **Ignoring the mine counter**: Always keep an eye on the remaining mine count. It is critical information for endgame logic.
3. **Random corner clicks**: If you must guess, do not click random corners — they are neither safer nor less safe than other unrevealed squares statistically.
4. **Missing cascades**: After each chord or reveal, scan all adjacent numbers again. Cascades of deductions are very common and easy to miss if you move too fast without looking.

## Practice Makes Perfect

The best way to internalise these patterns is repetition. Start on Beginner (8×8, 10 mines) and practise until you can clear it without guessing. Then move to Intermediate, then Expert. Each difficulty level teaches you to handle larger, denser boards.

Ready to put these strategies to the test? [Play Minesweeper on Puzzle PK now](/games/minesweeper) — challenge yourself in solo mode first, then take on a friend in real-time PK mode!

zh.content:
# 扫雷背后的隐藏逻辑：完整策略指南

大多数玩家把扫雷当成一款靠运气的游戏，随意乱点直到踩中地雷。但在这款看似简单的游戏外表之下，隐藏着一套**纯粹的逻辑与概率**体系。掌握这些技巧，你完全可以做到不靠猜测就稳定获胜。

## 理解基础规则

扫雷的核心规则极其简单：翻开格子上显示的数字，代表它**周围8个格子（横、竖、斜方向）中地雷的总数**。"1"意味着相邻格中只有一个地雷，"2"意味着两个。理解这一条规则，就是掌握一切的基础。

在进入具体技巧之前，先学会两个基本操作：
- **插旗**：当你确定某个格子是地雷时，右键点击插旗标记。
- **和弦展开（Chord）**：当一个数字格周围已标注的旗子数量恰好等于它的数字时，中键点击（移动端双击）会自动翻开所有未标记的邻格。这是游戏中最快的操作技巧。

## 必须掌握的核心模式

### 1-1 模式（墙边规律）

这是最常见的基础模式。当两个"1"紧靠着一面未翻开的"墙壁"时，**只有第二个"1"能看到、第一个"1"看不到的格子，必定安全**。

**举例**：`[1][1]`靠着三个未翻开的格子——最外侧的格子只属于其中一个"1"，因此地雷只可能在两个"1"共同相邻的内侧格子中。最外侧的格子可以安全点击。

这个模式可以延伸：沿墙出现`[1][1][1][1]`时，地雷呈现可预测的交替规律，让你能连锁清理大片区域。

### 1-2 模式（减法技巧）

当"1"和"2"相邻，且都紧靠同一面未翻开的墙时，你能获得强大的信息：

- "1"告诉你：我相邻的两个格子里，**恰好有一个**地雷。
- "2"告诉你：我相邻的三个格子里，**恰好有两个**地雷。
- 用减法推导：那个只有"2"能看到、"1"看不到的格子，**必定有一个地雷**。

掌握这种"两个约束相减"的减法思维，能解决绝大多数扫雷的推理难题。

### 1-2-1 模式（最可靠的公式）

当`[1][2][1]`沿着一面平整的墙排列时，**地雷必定在两个"1"正对面的格子里**，而"2"正对面的格子永远安全。这个规律极其可靠，几乎每局游戏都会出现。

### 1-2-2-1 模式

类似1-2-1，这个模式中地雷位于两个"2"的对面，而两个"1"对面的格子则是安全的。一旦你能瞬间识别这个图形，你会发现自己在几秒内就能破解整块区域。

## 角落与边缘策略

**角落**是强力的突破口。角落里的"1"在很多情况下只有一个相邻的未翻开格子，几乎直接告诉你地雷的位置。

**边缘格子**减少了每个数字能看到的邻格数量，让每个数字包含的信息更加精确。边缘出现的"3"约束性更强，往往更容易推导。

开局时，如果第一次点击翻出了空白格（数字为0），大片区域会自动级联翻开。建议点击**棋盘中央**——从统计上来说，这样最可能打开一大块空白区域，一次性揭示大量数字。

## 高级技巧：概率与计数

当纯逻辑推导用尽，必须猜测时，你仍然可以做出明智的选择。

### 地雷计数法

在游戏中任何时刻，你都能看到棋盘上的总地雷数（界面上的计数器）。随着你插旗标记地雷，计数器会相应减少。用总地雷数减去已插旗数，就知道剩余地雷数。当剩余未翻格数很少时，单凭算术就能确定所有地雷位置。

### 概率估算

被迫猜测时，估算概率而非盲目点击：
- 角落的孤立格子，地雷概率可能是50%（1/2）。
- 大片空白区域旁的开阔格子，基于整体地雷密度，概率可能只有10%~15%。
- 永远选择**概率最低**的格子点击。

### 边界分析法

高手会将棋盘分为"受约束格"（紧靠数字的未翻格）和"自由格"（完全不与任何数字相邻的未翻格）。自由格的地雷概率是均匀的：`剩余地雷数 ÷ 剩余自由格数`。将这个概率与受约束区域的计算概率相比较——有时候，开阔区域比看起来更安全。

## PK对战模式的速度技巧

在 Puzzle PK 的多人PK模式中，**速度与准确性同等重要**。以下是提速的专项技巧：

- **激进使用和弦展开**：每当你插旗标记了一个与数字格相邻的地雷，立刻对该数字格使用和弦展开。连锁展开会像多米诺骨牌一样扩散。
- **保持鼠标移动**：不要停下来长时间思考。快速扫描、标记显而易见的地雷、保持操作节奏。
- **左右键同时点击（经典和弦）**：在PC端，在一个地雷数已满足的数字格上同时按下左右键，会触发自动展开——比中键点击更快。
- **借助对手的翻开区域**：在PK争夺模式中，双方玩家共享同一棋盘。观察对手点击的位置——他们翻开的格子也给了你额外信息。

## 常见错误避免

1. **过度插旗**：很多玩家条件反射地标记每个可疑格。这会拖慢你的速度。只在需要用旗子触发和弦展开时才插旗。
2. **忽略地雷计数器**：时刻关注剩余地雷数，这是残局推理的关键信息。
3. **随机点角落**：如果必须猜测，不要优先点角落——从统计上看，角落和其他未翻格的地雷概率并无差别。
4. **错过连锁推导**：每次展开或插旗后，重新扫描所有相邻数字。连锁推导非常常见，操作过快时容易忽视。

## 熟能生巧

# Mastering 1A2B (Bulls and Cows): Strategy, Algorithms, and the Science of Deduction

1A2B — known internationally as Bulls and Cows, and also as Mastermind (in peg-colour form) — is one of the most elegant information theory puzzles ever devised. In its classic 4-digit form, you are trying to guess a 4-digit secret number (all digits unique, no zeros) in as few guesses as possible, using only the feedback you receive each round.

The feedback is deceptively simple:
- **A** (Bulls): How many digits are correct AND in the correct position.
- **B** (Cows): How many digits are correct but in the WRONG position.

For example, if the secret number is `4271` and you guess `1234`:
- The `2` is correct and in the correct position (position 2) → **1A**
- The `1` and `4` are correct but in wrong positions → **2B**
- Result: `1A2B`

From this single response, you need to extract maximum information to converge on the answer. Here is how to master that process.

## The Information-Theoretic View

Before diving into strategies, it helps to understand what 1A2B fundamentally is: an **information partitioning game**. Each guess you make divides all possible remaining secret numbers into groups, based on what feedback each would produce. The ideal guess is the one that makes these groups as equal in size as possible — minimising the worst-case number of remaining possibilities after you receive any response.

This is the same principle behind optimal binary search. You always want to cut the possibility space in half (or better), not just eliminate a few options.

There are exactly 5,040 possible 4-digit numbers with no repeated digits and no zeros (9 × 8 × 7 × 6 = 3,024 if we start from `1023` with zeros allowed, or 9 × 8 × 7 × 6 = 3,024 with `1` through `9`). A perfect player using information-optimal strategies can guarantee finding the answer in **5 guesses or fewer**.

## Stage 1: The Opening Guess

Your first guess should be designed to maximise information, not to make an intuitive "lucky" stab. Consider `1234` as an opening:

After `1234`, the response partitions all 5,040 possibilities into groups. No matter what response you receive, you will at minimum learn which (if any) of `1`, `2`, `3`, `4` are in the secret number and which positions they occupy.

Experienced players often use fixed opening sequences (like `1234` followed by `5678` if the response to `1234` is `0A0B`) to quickly determine which digits are in play before worrying about their exact positions.

## Stage 2: Digit Identification Phase

In the early rounds, your primary goal is to identify **which 4 digits appear in the secret number** (from the digits 1–9). With the digits identified, the problem collapses into a positional arrangement puzzle — which is far easier.

**Strategy**: Choose guesses that collectively cover all 9 possible digits (1–9) in as few guesses as possible. Guessing `1234` and then `5678` covers 8 digits in just 2 guesses. The combined feedback tells you definitively which digits are present:

- Any digit appearing in a "0A0B" response is **not** in the secret.
- Any digit contributing to A or B counts **is** in the secret.

After 2 strategic guesses, you typically know exactly which 4 digits are in play.

## Stage 3: Position Resolution

Once you know the digits, you need to determine their positions. With 4 known digits, there are at most 4! = 24 possible arrangements. Each guess eliminates a large fraction of these.

**Key technique — Systematic Transposition**: If you know the digits are `{1, 2, 7, 9}` and your guess `1279` returns `2A2B`, you know 2 digits are correctly placed and 2 are swapped. Systematically swap pairs of suspected wrong-position digits until the arrangement locks into place.

**Exploit pure A responses**: A guess that returns `4A0B` is the secret — you are done. A response of `3A0B` means exactly one digit is misplaced. Since you know which 3 are correct, the misplaced one must swap into the remaining position.

## Advanced Technique: Constraint Tracking

Maintain a running list of constraints after each guess. Every response rules out an enormous number of arrangements. The key is to be systematic rather than intuitive:

1. **Positive constraints**: "Digit 7 IS in the number." (from any A or B count)
2. **Negative constraints**: "Digit 3 is NOT in the number." (from 0A0B responses involving 3)
3. **Positional constraints**: "Digit 5 is NOT in position 2." (from B contributions)
4. **Fixed constraints**: "Digit 9 IS in position 3." (from A contributions)

By tracking these constraints methodically, you can verify each candidate guess against everything you know before making it. Any guess that is inconsistent with a known constraint is wasted information.

## The Minimax Algorithm (How Computers Do It)

If you want to understand the truly optimal approach, it is the **minimax algorithm**:

1. Generate all remaining possible secrets (consistent with all prior feedback).
2. For each candidate guess, simulate what response each possible secret would produce.
3. Count the size of the largest response group (worst case).
4. Choose the guess that minimises this worst-case group size.

This approach guarantees that you always reduce the possibility space as aggressively as possible. Computers using minimax can solve any 1A2B puzzle in at most 5 guesses, with an average of around 4.3 guesses.

You do not need to run the full algorithm mentally, but internalising its principle — "choose guesses that hurt you least in the worst case" — will significantly improve your intuitive play.

## Reading Feedback Like a Detective

Think of each 1A2B response as evidence in a detective case. Good detectives do not jump to conclusions from a single clue; they build a web of mutually reinforcing evidence.

**"0A0B"** is not bad news — it is *excellent* information. It eliminates every digit in your guess from consideration.

**"4A0B"** means you have solved the puzzle. 

**"0A4B"** is one of the most tantalising responses: all 4 of your digits are correct, but all 4 are in the wrong position. There is exactly one arrangement that maps to this feedback — find it.

**Avoid confirmation bias**: If you have a strong guess in mind, verify it against *all* previous feedback, not just the most recent. It is easy to check only the last clue and miss an earlier contradiction.

## PK Mode Strategy: Speed vs. Optimality

In Puzzle PK's competitive 1A2B PK mode, your opponent is racing against you in real time. The optimal strategy shifts slightly:

- **Speed matters more than optimality**: Making a fast 80%-optimal guess is often better than taking 10 extra seconds to compute the perfect one.
- **Watch your opponent**: In PK mode, you can observe how many guesses your opponent has made. If they are on guess 3 and you are on guess 2, take a more conservative (information-maximising) approach. If they are ahead, consider a slightly riskier "lucky guess" that could end the game instantly.
- **Pattern recognition over calculation**: At high skill levels, experienced players have memorised common feedback patterns and their implications. Practise until the "digit identification phase" becomes automatic.

## Practice Recommendations

**Start with 3-digit practice**: Try 3A0B (3 unique digits from 1–7) before moving to the full 4-digit game. The strategy is identical but the reduced complexity lets you internalise the feedback interpretation without cognitive overload.

**Self-analyse your guesses**: After each game, review your guess sequence. Could any guess have been replaced by one with higher information value? This retrospective analysis is the fastest path to improvement.

**Play regularly**: The pattern-matching instincts and constraint-tracking habits develop best through repetition. Even 5–10 games per week will produce noticeable improvement within a month.

Ready to test your deductive skills? [Play 1A2B (Codebreaker) on Puzzle PK](/games/codebreaker) — challenge yourself in solo mode or face a real opponent in real-time PK!

zh.keywords: 1A2B, 猜数字, 密码战, 算法, 策略, 信息论
zh.author: Puzzle PK 团队
zh.content:
# 精通 1A2B（猜数字）：策略、算法与演绎推理的艺术

1A2B——国际上称为"公牛与母牛（Bulls and Cows）"，也是棋盘版"猜色游戏（Mastermind）"的数字变体——是有史以来设计最优雅的信息论谜题之一。经典的4位数形式中，你需要用尽可能少的猜测次数，猜出一个4位数的秘密数字（各位数字不重复，不含0），所能利用的只有每轮猜测后收到的反馈。

反馈规则极其简单：
- **A（公牛）**：数字正确且位置正确的位数。
- **B（母牛）**：数字正确但位置错误的位数。

举例：如果秘密数字是 `4271`，你猜 `1234`：
- `2` 正确且在第2位 → **1A**
- `1` 和 `4` 正确但位置错误 → **2B**
- 结果：`1A2B`

仅凭这一条反馈，你需要提取最大信息量来逼近答案。以下是掌握这个过程的方法。

## 信息论视角

在进入具体策略之前，先理解1A2B的本质：这是一个**信息划分游戏**。你每猜一次，就把所有可能的秘密数字按"如果是它的话会返回什么反馈"分成若干组。理想的猜测，是让这些组尽可能均等——无论得到哪种反馈，都能把可能的数量削减到最低。

这与二分查找的最优策略原理完全相同：你总是想把可能空间砍成两半，而不是每次只排除几个选项。

4位数字均不重复且不含0的秘密数字共有 9×8×7×6 = 3,024 种（若包含0则为5,040种）。使用信息最优策略的完美玩家，能保证在**5次或更少**的猜测内找到答案。

## 第一阶段：开局猜测

首次猜测应设计为最大化获取信息，而不是凭直觉猜一个"感觉对"的数字。以 `1234` 作为开局：

无论得到什么反馈，你都会至少知道 `1`、`2`、`3`、`4` 中哪些在秘密数字里，以及它们是否在正确位置。

经验丰富的玩家通常使用固定的开局序列：比如先猜 `1234`，如果返回 `0A0B`，再猜 `5678`，从而快速确认哪些数字在局内，再考虑位置问题。

## 第二阶段：数字识别期

在前几轮中，首要目标是确认**哪4个数字出现在秘密数字中**（从1~9里选4个）。一旦确定了数字集合，问题就变成了一个纯粹的位置排列谜题——这要容易得多。

**策略**：选择能集体覆盖所有9个数字（1~9）的猜测序列，尽量用最少的次数。猜 `1234` 然后 `5678`，两次就覆盖了8个数字：

- 出现在 `0A0B` 反馈中的任何数字，**不在**秘密数字里。
- 对A或B计数有贡献的任何数字，**在**秘密数字里。

经过2次策略性猜测，通常就能确切知道哪4个数字在局内。

## 第三阶段：位置确定

确认数字后，需要确定它们的位置。4个已知数字有最多 4! = 24 种排列方式，每次猜测可以排除其中很大一部分。

**核心技巧——系统性换位**：假设你知道数字集合是 `{1, 2, 7, 9}`，猜测 `1279` 返回 `2A2B`，说明有2个数字位置正确，2个位置错误。系统地交换你怀疑位置错误的数字对，直到所有位置锁定。

**利用纯A反馈**：返回 `4A0B` 就意味着猜中了，游戏结束。返回 `3A0B` 意味着恰好有一个数字错位——由于你知道哪3个位置正确，那个错位的数字必然要移到唯一剩余的位置。

## 高级技巧：约束条件追踪

每次猜测后维护一份约束条件清单。每条反馈都排除了大量的排列可能。关键是系统性地追踪，而不是靠直觉：

1. **正向约束**："数字7在秘密数字中。"（来自任何包含7且返回A或B的猜测）
2. **负向约束**："数字3不在秘密数字中。"（来自包含3但返回0A0B的猜测）
3. **位置约束**："数字5不在第2位。"（来自5贡献B计数的猜测）
4. **固定约束**："数字9在第3位。"（来自9贡献A计数的猜测）

系统追踪这些约束，让你在下每一次猜测之前都能验证它是否与所有已知信息相符。任何与已知约束矛盾的猜测，都是浪费的信息量。

## 极小极大算法：计算机的做法

如果你想理解真正最优的方法，那就是**极小极大（Minimax）算法**：

1. 生成所有与之前反馈相符的可能秘密数字列表。
2. 对于每个候选猜测，模拟每个可能秘密数字会产生什么反馈。
3. 计算最大反馈组的大小（最坏情况）。
4. 选择使最坏情况组最小的猜测。

这种方法保证每次猜测都能最激进地削减可能空间。使用极小极大算法的计算机，可以在最多5次猜测内解决任何1A2B谜题，平均约4.3次。

你不需要在脑海中运行完整算法，但内化其核心原则——"在最坏情况下伤害最小的猜测是最好的"——将显著提升你的直觉判断水平。

## 像侦探一样解读反馈

把每次1A2B反馈当作侦探案件中的证据。好的侦探不会从单一线索跳到结论，而是构建相互印证的证据网络。

**"0A0B"** 不是坏消息——而是**极好的**信息。它一次性排除了你猜测中的所有数字。

**"4A0B"** 意味着你已经解开了谜题。

**"0A4B"** 是最令人兴奋的反馈之一：你的4个数字全部正确，但全部在错误位置。将4个数字完全重排，找到唯一满足的排列。

**避免确认偏误**：当你脑海中有一个强烈的候选猜测时，要检验它是否符合**所有**之前的反馈，而不仅仅是最近一条。只看最新线索很容易忽略更早的矛盾。

## PK对战模式策略：速度vs.最优性

在 Puzzle PK 的1A2B竞技对战中，对手与你同时竞速。最优策略略有不同：

- **速度有时比最优性更重要**：快速做出一个80%最优的猜测，通常比花10秒计算完美猜测更有价值。
- **观察对手**：PK模式中你能看到对手猜了几次。如果对手在第3次猜测，而你才到第2次，采取更保守（信息最大化）的方法。如果对手领先，考虑一个稍具冒险性的"幸运猜测"，说不定能一击即中。
- **图案识别优于临场计算**：高水平玩家已记住了常见反馈模式及其含义。反复练习，直到"数字识别阶段"变成肌肉记忆。

## 练习建议

**先练3位数版本**：在进入完整的4位数游戏前，先玩3位数版本（从1~7中选3个不重复数字）。策略完全相同，但复杂度更低，让你能在不超载认知的情况下内化反馈解读。

**复盘自己的猜测**：每局结束后，回顾你的猜测序列。有哪次猜测可以换成信息量更高的选择？这种事后分析是最快的提升路径。

**定期练习**：图案匹配的直觉和约束追踪的习惯，通过重复训练发展最快。即使每周5~10局，一个月内就能看到明显进步。

准备好测试你的演绎能力了吗？[在 Puzzle PK 玩1A2B（密码战）](/games/codebreaker)——单人挑战模式磨练技巧，或与真实对手进行实时PK对决！

# Why Playing Sudoku Every Day is Good for Your Brain

You have probably seen Sudoku grids in newspapers, apps, and puzzle books for years. But is playing a number puzzle every day actually beneficial, or is it just a pleasant way to pass the time? The science might surprise you.

A growing body of research links regular Sudoku practice to measurable improvements in memory, concentration, problem-solving speed, and — most compellingly — a reduced risk of age-related cognitive decline. Here is a detailed look at what happens to your brain when you make Sudoku part of your daily routine.

## 1. Strengthens Working Memory

Working memory is your brain's short-term "scratchpad" — the mental workspace where you hold and manipulate information while performing a task. It is what lets you remember the start of a sentence while reading its end, or keep track of a calculation while performing it mentally.

Sudoku is an extremely effective workout for working memory. To solve a puzzle efficiently, you must simultaneously:
- Remember which numbers you have already placed in each row, column, and 3×3 box.
- Keep track of candidate numbers for multiple cells at once.
- Update your mental notes as you fill in each new number.

Studies on working memory training consistently show that the skills gained in puzzle-solving transfer to improved performance on unrelated memory tasks — a phenomenon known as **cognitive transfer**. Daily Sudoku practice is, in effect, a gym session for your mental workspace.

## 2. Builds Logical Reasoning and Deductive Thinking

Every Sudoku puzzle is a closed logical system with a unique solution. Every deduction you make — "the number 7 cannot go in this cell because it is already in this row" — is a pure application of logical inference.

Over time, regular Sudoku practice ingrains a **deductive reasoning habit**: the instinct to gather constraints, eliminate impossibilities, and converge on the only remaining option. This habit of thinking is directly applicable to debugging software, analysing arguments, troubleshooting mechanical problems, and any domain where structured reasoning from evidence matters.

Unlike trivia or memory games, Sudoku does not train you to recall facts. It trains you to *think clearly* — a far more portable and durable cognitive skill.

## 3. Improves Focus and Attention to Detail

Solving a Sudoku puzzle requires maintaining attention across a 9×9 grid for anywhere from five minutes to an hour, depending on difficulty. Your eye must scan systematically, your mind must avoid distraction, and you must notice — immediately — when a number placed in one cell creates a contradiction elsewhere.

In the era of constant notifications and fragmented attention, this kind of **sustained, systematic attention** is increasingly rare and valuable. Regular Sudoku players report noticeably improved ability to focus on tasks at work and in study, with fewer errors caused by missed details.

Research on attentional training suggests this is not simply anecdotal: activities that require sustained, goal-directed attention (like puzzle solving) produce measurable improvements in attentional control over time.

## 4. Reduces Stress and Promotes a Mindful State

Here is a benefit that surprises many people: Sudoku is an effective **stress-reduction tool**.

When you are deeply engaged in solving a logic puzzle, your mind is fully occupied by the present task. There is no bandwidth left for rumination about past regrets or future anxieties. This state of complete cognitive absorption — what psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi famously described as **"flow"** — is associated with reduced cortisol levels (the stress hormone), improved mood, and a sense of calm satisfaction.

Many regular Sudoku players describe their daily puzzle as a form of active meditation: it quiets the inner noise of daily life without requiring you to sit still and "clear your mind" — a task most people find genuinely difficult.

## 5. May Help Delay Cognitive Decline

This is perhaps the most compelling finding from Sudoku research. A long-term study published in the *International Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry* found that adults aged 50 and over who regularly engage in number puzzles (including Sudoku and crosswords) show cognitive function equivalent to people about 10 years younger than their chronological age.

The underlying mechanism is the **cognitive reserve** hypothesis: the more your brain is actively exercised throughout life, the more neural connections it builds, and the more resilient it becomes to age-related damage. Regular puzzle-solving is thought to be one of the most accessible ways to build cognitive reserve without any special equipment or expertise.

## 6. Accessible, Screen-Safe, and Infinitely Scalable

One of Sudoku's greatest practical advantages is its scalability. Whether you are a complete beginner who needs 30 minutes to solve an Easy grid, or an expert who can crack a Diabolical puzzle in under 10 minutes, the cognitive challenge adjusts perfectly to your level.

Unlike many brain-training apps that rely on novelty and gradually become boring, Sudoku's endless variety of puzzle configurations means each game presents genuinely new constraints to reason through. The game never gets "stale" — it gets deeper.

## How to Build a Daily Sudoku Habit

The most effective approach is to **anchor Sudoku to an existing daily routine**. Play one Easy puzzle with your morning coffee. Spend 10 minutes on a Medium puzzle during your lunch break. Tackle a Hard puzzle before bed as a wind-down activity.

Start with the difficulty level where you feel challenged but not overwhelmed — typically Easy or Medium for newcomers. As your pattern recognition improves over weeks, progressively step up the difficulty.

Consistency matters far more than duration. One 10-minute puzzle daily, done reliably, will produce more lasting cognitive benefits than sporadic marathon sessions.

## Start Today

Ready to give your brain its daily workout? [Play free Sudoku on Puzzle PK](/games/sudoku) — no download, no registration required. Choose Easy mode to build your foundations, or challenge a friend in our real-time PK mode for an extra competitive edge. Your brain will thank you in ten years.
